titleStmt.title: Interview with Louis E. Spitzfaden, Undated
titleStmt.author: Thomas J. Healy II

projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Louis E. Spitzfaden was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Now, I'm just going to ask you if -- just tell me your -- tell me your name -- just, I want you to say your name, "Dover, Delaware," and then tell me, "I was born in wherever on such a date. I grew up here. I did this." Just tell me a little story.

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: My name is Lou Spitzfaden.

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: Oh, sorry. You need to swing the microphone, please. Sorry. Right there. Is that good?

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: Yeah. Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay. I'm sorry. Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: My name is Lou Spitzfaden. I was born in New York City, grew up in the Queensboro section of New York City, and entered into the Marine Corps in January of 1943. I was almost honored in a way to be selected by the Marine Corps to go to the U.S. Naval and Bomb Disposal School. And that is a story of its own because during the war, it was something new for all the military services, the bomb disposal business. Actually, it was a forerunner to today's bomb squads that are manned mostly by the police departments in the large cities. Of course, back then, we never heard of bomb disposal, no less a bomb squad in a city.

However, to get back to the selection for this school, at that time, we even had British officers teaching us the art of bomb disposal because the bombs fell in London during the war and many of them didn't go off. They were known as duds. So -- and they were in populated areas, a very dangerous situation. So they had to be neutralized. Some way of getting to these explosive objects, you might say -- it was more than bombs -- so that they wouldn't go off and kill a lot of civilian personnel. And that was the birth of bomb disposal.

It takes in more than bombs. I keep mentioning that word, but we also neutralize projectiles, artillery projectiles, landmines, torpedos. That's the Navy's job. And sea mines that didn't go off. Anything holding an explosive element that did not operate as one might think it should have operated; however, that's not the case. The various fuses in these devices were many. Some were point-detonating fuses. Then if the object hit its target, it went off immediately. Some were time-delay fuses, and that's what created a problem. And among the time-delay fuses, you had a mechanical time delay, you had an electrical time delay, you had a chemical time delay. It was just something that we didn't know in the beginning what we were doing.

It was a matter of experimenting and -- well, people look at people like me and say, "What were you doing in such a category of" -- I can't answer that question. We were all volunteers. I was 18 years of age at the time, as many of my colleagues. And we did it. It was a job that had to be done, and that -- that was the bottom line.

Later on, that bomb disposal community got to be known as EOD, explosive ordinance disposal. So that took in all of the explosive munitions to be disposed of, regardless of how it came about, but we had to get rid of the hazard. And I -- today, I belong to the National EOD Association. And we keep close contact with each other because we've all gone through this.

It's a very unique organization. In fact, I'm proud to be a past commander. I believe it was 1990-'91 or '92. I don't remember. But still active today, and we share our war experiences among that organization, different parts of the world. Speaking of different parts of the world, we have to know not only U.S. ammunition, but the enemy's ammunition and the allied ammunition, Russian, German, Italian, Chinese, Japanese, Korean, the markings on their munitions. We have manuals that keep us abreast of it, and not only that, but they refresh our memory. It can't be memorized. We have to have references to that type of ordinance.

And basically, I believe the public should know this. We keep on going through our national organization, but the average citizen except for the local bomb squad, the police bomb squad, really doesn't realize that the military is still involved in it. In fact, we're involved in it very heavily at the present time over in Iraq.

And I get reports on EOD personnel, male and female today, that are KIAs, killed in action. Only this past 10 to 15 days, we've had four killed-in-action reports. And -- well, it's a story that should be told, and I'm here to tell it. And I believe I have unless there's any questions.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Tell me a little bit about [inaudible] -- you went to -- okay. You were born in New York?

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: And right out of high school, you went in?

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Did you go to --

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: -- truthfully, I quit high school to go in --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: -- to go in, as did many of my schoolmates at the time. I enlisted. I was 17 years of age. I guess I broke my mother's heart because she had to sign my enlistment papers. And today, I realize it was a hard, hard thing for her to do. And going back to the old neighborhood, leaving at 17 years of age, I have never gone back to New York City to live. From there, it was traveling with the military, all together for 27 years. And then seeing greener grass, I guess you would say. And here I ended up in Delaware. That happened because of a military assignment when I was assigned to Aberdeen, Maryland and had to come into Dover, Delaware area as an instructor for radiological monitoring. And that was in the early '60s. And we were teaching state police and fire personnel, fire department, firefighters and some teachers and nurses how to use the instruments for radiological monitoring for the fallout.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: You mean our Geiger counters that we had on our rescue trucks?

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: There you go. Yes, sir. And at that time, it was a very popular subject, you might say.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: The fallout shelters were being built, et cetera, et cetera. But that's the first time I came to Dover, and truthfully, I liked what I saw. And I promised myself that when I retire, that's going to be it. And it was. So I've been here since 1976. Actually, it's been the longest time I've ever spent in one place in my entire life. But I enjoy every minute of it.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: What did -- tell me a little bit of -- what did -- what did your mom and dad do, or what did your dad do? Or were you born -- you were born in New York.

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: I was born in New York.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Were your parents -- were your parents born in the United States or were they --

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: Yes, they were. It was the grandparents that came over from Germany. I was second generation, U.S. born. My father was a factory worker, laborer. My mother, for most of her life, was a housewife and mother. At one time, she was a long distance operator for the telephone company, but that was way before my time.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Where in -- where in New York did you live? Or in Manhattan?

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: I did not live in Manhattan. I say New York as New York City.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Right, okay.

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: And it has five boroughs.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Yes, it does. And you're absolutely right.

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: Right. And we lived in Queensboro, in a section of Queens called Ridgewood. And after my public school, I -- well, that's what started this bomb disposal business. I attended Brooklyn Technical High School, very renowned high school for technical training and engineering. But -- I don't know whether foolishly or just gung-ho or what you want to call it, but I gave them three and a half years and never finished because I wanted to go fight in the war.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Well, I think you have -- so you remem -- you remember Pearl Harbor Day?

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: Very well.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay. So tell me -- answer me -- when you're -- when you're -- when you're -- when I ask you a question, sort of repeat it with that same question because nobody's going to hear me in the documentary. They're going to hear your answer.

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So -- so they know what you're talking about, say, "I remember Pearl Harbor Day because" --

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: Well, I remember Pearl Harbor Day. I was out with a gang of my neighborhood playmates, you might say. And we didn't believe what we heard over the radio. And then of course it was confirmed later in the evening. And my dad, who was a veteran of World War I, the 77th Division, Statue of Liberty Division, was almost uncontrollable. And I believe that's what had the biggest effect -- excuse me -- the biggest effect on me.

And I couldn't wait to defend my country. He would have signed the papers right away. It was Mom that held back a little bit. But I mentioned Brooklyn Tech High School because it seemed that I had two major assignments in the Marine Corps during the war. One was as -- as a company armorer, and I went to small arms repair school in Philadelphia. Right off the Schuylkill River was a warehouse where they were holding the classes. And my first overseas assignment was Puerto Rico.

I was the company armorer at a base called Roosevelt Roads. And a lot of people have today heard about Ro -- we call Rosie Roads, but the Marines were down there in the beginning while it was being built. And we were the guard company. And later on during the construction, we -- the Marines left and turned everything over to the Navy, including the guard duty.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Thank God. Just kidding. I'm a Navy man.

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: All right. So -- well, from there, I was transferred to Quantico, Virginia. And being the small arms repair type and so forth, I was assigned to the small arms company of the training battalion and taught the officer candidates different weapons and how to fire them and so forth. That's when my orders came through for bomb disposal school.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Now, what did you -- so you enlisted right in the Marine Corps? How did you do that? Tell me how you got in.

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: You went down. You decided you wanted to join.

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: Well, you see, getting back to Pearl Harbor, that was in December of '42.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: '1. December '41.

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: '41. Excuse me.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: That's okay.

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: Yeah. That's where the mind goes as you age.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: ?That's fine, too.?

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: All right. December '41. And I wasn't of age then at all, but in December of '42, I was 17 years of age. And I went down to the recruiting station, and they did what you might call a preliminary enlistment. That was December 14. It was a year and seven days after Pearl Harbor. And they told us, "Well, now go home." This is the Marine Corps. "Go home. Enjoy the holidays because it might be the last you ever see."

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Nice.

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: Yeah. And I got called to active duty January 28, 1943.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Then where did you go to boot camp?

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: Parris Island. Right on down to Parris Island. And I guess I am one of a kind because I did enjoy it. Later on in my career, I was a drill instructor at Parris Island during the Korean War. And it just goes on. It was in my blood, and that was it.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Did -- so -- I've got a Marine question to ask you. What -- was there many Marines over in the European Theater?

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: Well, we're talking about assignments with the Marine Corps. I never was assigned to Europe. All of my time, even after the war, was done in the Pacific, to include, during peacetime, Okinawa and Hawaii and Japan. But I never had an assignment in Europe.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Was -- was there any battles that the Marines played any major -- over in Europe? Or were they more -- it was more South Pacific, right?

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: South Pacific, yeah. And as I say -- the Marines were -- weren't over in Europe to any extent. They were. There were some there, but the Marine Corps did most of their battles and war games in South Pacific. Some of the people listening to me today can remember Guadalcanal, Tarawa, Saipan, Tinian, Wake Island, the Marshall Islands, on into Okinawa. I was on Guam when the Japanese surrendered. We were ready to make the invasion of Tokyo. In fact, I lost all of my personal gear at Guam. It was already packed. It was on the ship. The ship got lost somewhere, and my and other comrades' gear was lost, but we weren't. We didn't make the invasion. And that of course was from the atomic bombs that they dropped. People scoff, say things about the atomic bombs that we used, not realizing that had we not used them, how many lives would have been lost on the invasion of Japan. I mean, that goes without saying. It would have been in the thousands.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So after -- where was your -- where -- what was your first duty assignment after your bomb disposal when you got into all that? Were you assigned overseas?

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah. After finishing bomb disposal school, of course there was a transition period, but then I found myself over at Camp Pendleton, which was a staging area for the Marine Corps, and -- as I said before, that was out to the South Pacific to do your job. And I was assigned to two major commands. One was the 3rd Amphib Corps, Amphibious Corps, and the other was the 5th Amphibious Corps. Well, each Marine Corps headquarters had three divisions under them. So in essence, the bomb disposal people worked from corps headquarters, but supported all six divisions, wherever they may be headed at the time. And I was assigned to an MEIU team, and don't ask me what that stood for -- stands for anymore. But that was a Navy unit. And that was on Guam. Well, the Navy and the Marine worked together, and then we had a division of how we worked, which was the high watermark. Well, of course, if this dud was below the high watermark, it belonged to the Navy. Above the high watermark, it was dry land, and it belonged to the Marine Corps. Well, we kept raising that high watermark up, up the beach all the time, but that's getting back to the jovial side. And that, we did a lot of. We had to do. In fact, bomb disposal technicians -- I don't think they use it anymore today. It was a little gross, but they used to tell us, "That's one way to get up in the world." It's bad. As I say, I don't hear that expression anymore. I might add to that that they have on display in their museums as antiques, the tools and the equipment that we used to experiment with as something new to do the job that we have to do. And to try to keep up with today's technology, I know I can't do it. And I know a lot of my colleagues can't do it, of my age. But I admire the young people today to carry on and even to get involved, to volunteer for an explosive ordinance disposal position.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Tell me about -- you got out in -- when? '46?

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: I got out in nine -- after the war, they had the point system. You had so many points, you could get out. Well, I did get out. I got out in '46. I was discharged from Great Lakes naval air station and took -- what we had then was the ruptured duck, and that duck and I ran as far as we could. However, I broke my lifetime by six years' civilian time. I went back into the military. As I say, it's in me. And it's not for everybody. I also did a small stint as a recruiting sergeant. And you never want to force anybody into a military career. Even parents should not force their sons or daughters because if you're -- if you're there without self-motivation, more than likely, you're going to get messed up. So it takes a certain person.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Now, did you -- did you retire from the Marines?

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Tell me about that.

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: But you can, if you get that. I keep referring to my time in the military, 27 years, and I did 12 years with the United States Marine Corps, and the other 15, I did with the United States Army. And I made the transition for personal reasons, more than anything else. One of the obvious reasons was that knowing that I was going to make a career of the military, I thought I -- at that time, I could go a little bit further with my rank for retirement by switching to the Army, which I did.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: And that assigned you to Aberdeen? Is that where you ended up?

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: My first assignment with the Army was a choice assignment. I could choose my first assignment. So I said, "Well, are there any" -- EOD at that time, not bomb disposal. "Are there any EOD billets open in Hawaii?" I was shooting for the stars. Recruiter says, "Yes. You want to go to Hawaii?" Well, we did. My family and I went to Hawaii, my wife and three daughters. And then I had a further choice of flying to Hawaii or going by ship. And I elected to go by ship. And it was a beautiful voyage. And we all enjoyed three years of Hawaiian sunshine. My oldest daughter graduated high school in Hawaii, something she'll never forget. And of course I took them to other places since then, but that was the beginning of my Army career.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Not a bad start.

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: No. Not at all.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: And how ac -- how active did you stay -- well, you say you still are keeping up with the disposal part, right? Or the --

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: With the association. Not -- not with the work. No. I don't know if you'd want me to expand on that.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: It's just it's a very interesting -- I mean, today -- in today's world, there's -- you know, just like you said, there's so many -- so many options that -- with this disposal.

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: And it's -- I know because I'm -- I'm a fire -- I'm a firefighter also, but with the homeland security stuff, you just -- so many different things that can go on.

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: Oh, to the equipment they --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: So much you need to know.

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. It's mind-boggling to me. I wouldn't even want to start it over again.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: And it was bad enough when we went through at that time, learning the foreign ordinance and so forth.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Well, it -- but you had a pretty interesting -- I did -- we did a bunch of work before Iraq, film-wise, at -- down at Aberdeen. We had no clue what we were doing until Iraq came out. I mean, we had no idea why we were doing the stuff for the Bradleys and why we were doing this and why we were doing that. And we had -- I mean, the passes then. We had the passes when we were outside. We had to keep the passes covered up. I mean, it was just a whole bunch of different stuff. We had no clue.

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: Oh, it's gotten ridiculous.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: I was in the Navy, and I was in -- I had the highest security clearance in there, and it was like need to know. And so -- I mean, we were there to do a job, and we did it. But what's interesting is, is all the stuff that's over there as far as the, you know, the Russia in this and the Iraqi in this and, you know, all the different types of -- of -- of weaponry and -- and -- and grenades and bombs and --

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: They have to be up on them.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: -- and trucks and cars and everything. How they just tear it apart and look at it. It's just ab -- it just absolutely amazes me.

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: Well, I'll tell you a little story that I got two days ago, talking to a master sergeant from Indiantown Gap, and this was over at the mortuary at the base. Another one of our EOD people passed through. So I was there with him and talking. And he said the one that he remembers and called his helper away from, there was a dog laying on the side of the road, and some of the sand and the debris got blown away from the dog -- dead dog, by the way -- from the dog. And they saw two wires coming out of it. And the EOD tech was going to check that out, to see if it was an improvised explosive device. And it had an anti-disturbance fuse. Had he even stepped close to that dog, it would have blown him to kingdom come.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Amazing. Tell me, what would your message be or what's your message for the future generations about World War II?

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: What do we do? Say this in conclusion?

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: No. Go ahead. Just -- I just want your feelings about it towards -- you know, when you're on camera, you're going to be talking, and it's going to be what you feel -- you know, what you would like to pass on to future generations about you or about war.

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: Well, I guess as far as World War II is concerned, I said it more than once. All of my associates all volunteered. They all enlisted. We had a draft at that time, and the gang that I hung out with thought it was a disgrace to be drafted, so they enlisted in the Navy, the Marines, the Army. Coast Guard. I had two -- two very close friends in the Coast Guard. All enlistees, most of us 17 years of age. And there's something that I smile at today. I don't want to belittle the -- what's going on in Iraq, but -- well, let me -- let me put it this way. When we enlisted, we enlisted for the duration and six, which meant you're in as long as the war lasts plus six months until we can get you home and get you back where you started from. And for the majority of the active duty people, they were away from home for that three, four years. They didn't even get a leave during that time. It was continuous active duty. And I smile when I read about three-month deployments and six-month deployments. I don't know if I'm stepping on anyone's toes here, but the logical part of this short deployment -- and now we're getting into politics, I guess -- is doesn't anyone realize how much it costs to rotate fighting forces every three months, alone? The shipping and -- and the gear and transportation and all the logistics involved. And then we fight about deficits. We -- I don't know. I guess I'm too old to understand that business. We went in. I said we went in for the duration and six. The duration could have been 12 years. Who knows? Plus the fact, getting back to my job in the military EOD, believe it or not, back then, we didn't even get any extra money for it. It was your job. We never thought twice about it. Today, they do get extra pay, hazardous duty pay. And they -- they deserve it. But back then, it wasn't heard of. It was another assignment. So I reflect on these things. What's good and what's bad? I wish that the up-and-coming generations do pay attention to what went on -- well, not only in World War II, but in World War I, too. It was just as, oh, dedicated during World War I. But we didn't think about leave time. We were there for the duration. We were fighting for our country. We had two wars going on, a war in Europe and a war in the Pacific. And it -- it had to be won. It had to protect the United States. And we all knew that. And we wanted our children to be protected and live the way they did live, in freedom and, for the most part, protected. The recent business with the Twin Towers, they said well, what were we protecting? Maybe I got to eat crow. But that's what we fought for. And I wish that all future generations would get more education on World War II, what it really was, and how their grandfathers and great-grandfathers felt about it. It wasn't a matter of, "Oh, do I have to go?" Or "Oh, do I want to go?" We went. There was a job to be done. We had an enemy that was a threat, and Pearl Harbor was evidence. Today, Twin Towers is evidence, but I don't have the information behind that today. I could say a lot, but I can't back up what I'm saying. But to the youth, to my grand -- to all -- all the up-and-coming generations, you should know the price of freedom, and that price was dear. A lot of people possibly hearing me today lost their grandfather during World War II or their great-grandfather. But I want them to realize that he did it willingly and for their sake. And we have all-volunteer services today. That's good. But they're all looking for more personnel. We don't have enough. And that's a statistic. They're all short of their quotas. I really don't have anything more to say.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: That's perfect. (Applause) Great.

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: Thank you.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Do you have anything?

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: How was it -- you got all the training to --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Look at me. If you can look --

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: You have all the training to work on these bombs. How was it when you had to really do it the first time? Is it just that -- did you just do what your training provided to you, or is it still a --

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: We felt --

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: -- very strange feeling, I can imagine.

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: Well, how can I get into this?

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: At least for a person who has -- who has not done this, it just appears to be quite a -- quite a suspenseful job.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Let me ask you the question. What was your first -- after school, after you were in for a while, what was your first real active assignment and how did you feel, meaning, "There's that bomb over there. We've got to detonate it, or we have to" -- right?

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: Yeah. What kind of protection did you have --

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: -- and --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Your first exper -- your real first experience is what --

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: I could --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: You say, "My real" --

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: Yeah. I can remember my first experience on -- on neutralizing a piece of ammunition, and this was my first assignment with the Army in Hawaii. And out in the pineapple fields, they used to turn up ammunition from World War I. And we got a call one day to go out to this field. And there was a mortar round. Well, they didn't know it was a mortar round, but when we got there, there was this object that was turned up in the -- in the -- what did I say? Pineapple field? I was wrong. This was a sugarcane field. But anyway, it got turned up, getting ready to plant or whatever they did. And it was a mortar round from World War I. And more than that, it was white phosphorous. Well, white phosphorous is a compound that when it hits the air, it bursts into flame, throws off a lot of sparks, a regular Fourth of July. So my partner and I approached it, and fortunately, he had done one before, but I hadn't. Now, I was confident that the team, he and I, would take care of it. But was I scared? Yes, I was. Because that old mortar round from World War II was so rusted that just one little flake of that rust dislodging while we're in the area and that -- the fireworks start. And you get burned by white phosphorous -- because many of our GIs did, but not too many of them lived to tell about it. Those burns go deep. And they go all over your body. So even though we had excellent training, and we were tested and retested, not only on paper, but practical exercises, that hesitancy is still there when you see the first dud. And another one -- well, I could go on and on, but there were times when -- I guess I just said to myself at that time, "What am I doing?" But we volunteered for it. It was my job, and I -- we did it. But yes. Well, you might want to cut this out, but at graduation, we were given a graduation present. So I was told about this. And I walked up to the line, and they handed me a brown bag, and that was my present with my certificate. So the present was a bottle of hair dye and a cork. Now you folks take it from there.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Do you have anything else?

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: Did you ever have one of these 500-pound bombs?

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: You'll have to repeat what he says.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Did -- did you ever have one of -- a big -- like a 500-pound bomb or anything that you had to do?

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: The largest piece of ordinance I ever destroyed was a 16-inch naval projectile. And that was lodged up in the mountains in the big island of Hawaii. And that was quite -- quite an experiment. Not an experiment, but quite interesting. To make sure that that naval projectile exploded, detonated this time, we used what is known as a shaped charge and a shaped charge concentrates the force almost to a pinhead going through the body of the projectile. And of course there are certain ways to place this shaped charge. And through our training and our education, on a naval projectile on back from the ogive and to the body of it, there's one point in the circumference of the projectile that's the thinnest part of the metal. Well, of course if you're going to penetrate any part of the metal, to make sure you're going to get the job done, you're going to go for the thinnest part. So that's where we placed that shaped charge. And put a time fuse on it and got in the Jeep very carefully and started down the mountainside and --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: And then took off like hell?

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: When we could. And then all of a sudden, ba-boom. But that was -- aside from -- excuse me -- aside from disposing of large piles of outdated ammunition and ammunition that might be hazardous because it was out in the elements or whatever the case may be. It wasn't safe for the troops to use. We would collect that ammunition and bring it off to a demolition site and then dispose of all of it with one big grand explosion, where it would all -- one would detonate the other. They were usually started with a fire, and as the fire heated up, these munitions would explode and explode and detonate each other. That's how we got rid of bad ammunition.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Okay. Do you want to do --

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: Sitting and looking?

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: I'm going to go check -- you're going to look right at my chair.

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: Don't look at him. Look right here like I'm here. I'm going to go see if this other man's here.

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: Do me a favor. Just pretend TJ is still sitting here. He's -- he would be about here, his head. I'll just take a still photograph of you. Several still photographs. Very good. Thank you, sir.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy II
sp.p: You did great.

sp.speaker: Louis E. Spitzfaden
sp.p: Oh, thank you. (Conclusion of interview)
